summary: Cameroon lies on the west coast of central Africa and, because of its geographic and cultural diversity, is called 'Africa in miniature'; both French and English are used within the country.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced in 1890 by German Pallottine missionaries, when Cameroon was a German colony (1884–1916). After the First World War Cameroon was divided between Britain and France as mandate territories, and the Catholic Church in the French mandate expanded rapidly with the support of the colonial authorities, with church schools becoming the main providers of education. Today Catholicism is the largest religion, found mainly in the central, southern and western regions.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced in 1845 by the English Baptist missionary Alfred Saker in the Douala area, the earliest Christian missionary activity in Cameroon. During the German colonial period the Basel Mission was active in the west and coastal areas, and the Protestant churches of the British mandate also had great influence. Today Protestants are concentrated mainly in the English-speaking areas of the west, northwest and southwest and in coastal cities.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced to the north in the early 19th century with the jihad movement of the Fulani; from 1804 Usman dan Fodio launched a jihad in what is now northern Nigeria, and the Fulani then founded the Adamawa Emirate, which ruled northern Cameroon. Today Muslims are concentrated mainly in Adamawa, the North and the Far North regions of the north, and King Ibrahim Njoya of the Bamum Kingdom in the west also converted to Islam in the late 19th century.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: Other Christian denominations include Pentecostals, Evangelicals and indigenous independent churches. After Cameroon's political liberalization in the 1990s, Pentecostal and revival churches grew rapidly in cities, attracting large numbers of young people.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional beliefs center on ancestor worship, nature spirits and secret societies, and the chiefdoms of the western grassland region preserve rich traditional rituals and arts. Although only about 2% follow the traditional religion exclusively, many Christians and Muslims still take part in traditional rituals, such as the skull cult of the Bamileke.

religion.background: Before colonization Cameroon had the traditions of many peoples and religions: the north was Islamized under the influence of the Fulani jihad, while the south was mainly traditional belief. In 1845 English Baptist missionaries entered the coastal area, and after German colonization in 1884 Catholicism and the Basel Mission expanded their influence. After the First World War Cameroon was divided between Britain and France, each of which supported different churches and education systems. After independence and unification in 1960–1961, religion broadly took the distribution of Christians in the south and Muslims in the north, but relations between religions have generally been peaceful.

language.official: French and English are the official languages.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French became a main language when France took over eastern Cameroon after the First World War in 1916 (a League of Nations mandate from 1922), and became the official language after French Cameroon's independence in 1960. Because the French-speaking area makes up eight of the country's regions, including the capital Yaoundé and the economic center Douala, about 60% of the population use French as their main lingua franca.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English is spoken in the Northwest and Southwest regions of the west, an area under British mandate from 1916 to 1961 that merged with the French-speaking area after the 1961 plebiscite. Because the English-speaking area has a smaller population, its English-speaking residents have long complained of marginalization; in 2016 protests by lawyers and teachers against French-speaking judges and teachers entering the English-speaking area developed into a separatist conflict, called the 'Anglophone Crisis'.

language.history: Cameroon is called 'Africa in miniature' and has about 250 languages, including Bantu, Adamawa-Ubangi and Chadic languages. After German colonization in 1884 German was briefly the administrative language, and after the First World War, with Britain and France dividing the rule, French and English became the administrative languages of the two zones. In 1961 the two zones merged, and Cameroon became one of the few African countries with both English and French as official languages. Because of the many indigenous languages, cities have also developed 'Cameroonian Pidgin English' and 'Camfranglais', which mix English, French and indigenous languages and are very popular among young people.

ranking.name: Ndolé
ranking.description: A thick stew of bitter leaves (ndolé) cooked with peanut paste, beef, shrimp or dried fish, with a slight bitterness, often served with fried plantain or bâton de manioc (cassava sticks).
ranking.history: Ndolé originates from the traditional cuisine of the coastal Duala people; the bitter leaf is a local plant leaf that must be washed repeatedly to remove the bitterness. In the colonial period and after independence, the dish spread across the country as Douala became an economic center, and it is regarded as the national dish of Cameroon. It often appears at festivals, weddings and Sunday family meals, and every region has its own version.

ranking.name: Poulet DG (DG chicken)
ranking.description: Chicken is stir-cooked with fried plantain, carrot, green pepper, onion and tomato, colorful and richly flavored, a high-class dish for entertaining guests.
ranking.history: 'DG' is the abbreviation of the French 'directeur général' (director general); the dish appeared in restaurants in Douala and Yaoundé in the 1980s, when only high-earning corporate executives could afford such a lavish dish of chicken and plantain, hence the name. It reflects the economic prosperity and the emerging middle class brought by Cameroon's oil and cocoa exports in the 1970s–80s. Today it is a common dish at weddings and celebrations.

ranking.name: Eru
ranking.description: Finely shredded eru leaves (wild vine leaves) are stewed with waterleaf, palm oil, cow skin and dried fish, with a thick texture and a distinctive aroma.
ranking.history: Eru is a signature dish of the English-speaking Southwest Region, especially a traditional dish of the Bayangi people, and eru leaves are the leaves of a vine growing wild in the tropical rainforest. Because demand for wild eru leaves has increased greatly, overharvesting has appeared in recent years, and local people have begun to promote cultivation. It is often eaten with 'water fufu' made from cassava and is a cultural symbol of the people of the English-speaking region.

ranking.name: Achu soup
ranking.description: Taro is pounded into a yellow, purée-like staple, served with a bright yellow sauce made from palm oil, limestone water and spices, eaten by dipping with the fingers.
ranking.history: Achu soup is a traditional dish of the grassland area of the Northwest Region. The chiefdoms of the grassland area have a deep traditional culture, and achu soup has an important place at weddings, funerals and traditional festivals. Making it requires pounding the taro for hours and using a special limestone water to emulsify the palm oil into a bright yellow, a dish that shows off the skill of the housewife.

ranking.name: Puff-puff
ranking.description: Dough kneaded from flour, yeast and sugar is deep-fried into puffy small round balls, crisp outside and soft inside, often eaten with beans or chili sauce.
ranking.history: Puff-puff is common across West and Central Africa; in Nigeria and the English-speaking part of Cameroon it is called 'puff-puff', while in the French-speaking area it is called 'beignets'. Wheat flour entered Cameroon through trade in the colonial period and gradually became part of urban cuisine. Today 'puff-puff and beans' is the most common cheap breakfast in Cameroon, and the street stalls are mostly run by women.
